# Problem 1

```{r}
sales_raw <- tibble(
  sale_id = 1:8,
  customer_id = c("C1", "C2", "C1", "C3", "C2", "C4", "C5", "C2"),
  item_raw = c(" Pen", "PEN ", "Notebook", " pen ",
               "FOLDER", "Folder ", " ERASER ", "pen"),
  amount_raw = c("$10.00", "$20.00", NA, "$15.00",
                 "$30.00", "$25.00", NA, "$20.00"),
  discount_raw = c("0%", "10%", "5%", "0%", "20%", "10%", "0%", "0%"),
  code_raw = c("ST-101", "ON-102", "ST-103", "ON-104",
               "bad", "ST-106", "ON-107X", "on-108"),
  tags = c("gift;urgent", "online", "gift", "member",
           "online;member", "gift", "member", "gift;member")
)

```

# Problem A

```{r}
sales_clean <- sales_raw %>%
  mutate(
    item_clean = item_raw %>% str_trim() %>% str_squish() %>% str_to_lower(),
    amount = parse_number(amount_raw),
    discount_rate = parse_number(discount_raw) / 100,
    net_amount = amount * (1 - discount_rate),
    size = case_when(
      is.na(net_amount) ~ "unrecorded",
      net_amount >= 20 ~ "large",
      TRUE ~ "small"
    )
  )

print(sales_clean %>% select(sale_id, item_clean, amount, discount_rate, net_amount, size))

```
# Part B

```{r}

sales_codes <- sales_clean %>%
  mutate(
    code_clean = code_raw %>% str_trim() %>% str_to_upper(),
    valid_code = str_detect(code_clean, "^(ST|ON)-[0-9]{3}$")
  )
 
invalid_codes <- sales_codes %>%
  filter(!valid_code) %>%
  select(sale_id, code_raw, code_clean)
print(invalid_codes)

valid_code_parts <- sales_codes %>%
  filter(valid_code) %>%
  select(sale_id, code_clean) %>%
  separate_wider_delim(code_clean, delim = "-", names = c("channel", "number"),
                        cols_remove = FALSE)
print(valid_code_parts)
 
sale_tags <- sales_clean %>%
  select(sale_id, tags) %>%
  separate_longer_delim(tags, delim = ";")
print(sale_tags)

# separate_wider_delim() splits one column into several new columns while separate_longer_delim() splits a column text into multiple rows.


```


# Part C
```{r}

customer_summary <- sales_clean %>%
  summarise(
    sales_n = n(),
    known_n = sum(!is.na(net_amount)),
    large_n = sum(net_amount >= 20, na.rm = TRUE),
    large_share = if_else(known_n == 0, NA_real_, large_n / known_n),
    .by = customer_id
  ) %>%
  arrange(customer_id)
print(customer_summary)
 
# Numerator = 0.
# Denominator = 1.
# So C1's large_share = 0 / 1 = 0.
 
sales_factors <- sales_clean %>%
  mutate(
    item_factor = fct_infreq(factor(item_clean)),
    item_group = fct_lump_n(factor(item_clean), n = 2, other_level = "Other")
  )
print(levels(sales_factors$item_factor))
print(table(sales_factors$item_factor))
print(levels(sales_factors$item_group))
print(table(sales_factors$item_group))


```


# Problem 2

```{r}

reports_raw <- tibble(
  form = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B"),
  line = c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3),
  customer_id = c("C1", NA, "C2", "C3", NA, "C4"),
  round = c(1, 3, 1, 1, 2, 1),
  primary_amount = c(10, -999, 20, NA, 0, 30),
  backup_amount = c(NA, 15, 25, NA, 99, NA)
)
 
customers <- tibble(
  customer_id = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "C5"),
  region = c("North", "South", NA, "West")
)


```


# Part A

```{r}

reports_labeled <- reports_raw %>%
  arrange(form, line) %>%
  group_by(form) %>%
  fill(customer_id, .direction = "down") %>%
  ungroup()
print(reports_labeled)
 
reports_clean <- reports_labeled %>%
  mutate(
    primary_clean = na_if(primary_amount, -999),
    amount = coalesce(primary_clean, backup_amount)
  )
print(reports_clean %>% select(form, line, customer_id, round, primary_amount, backup_amount, amount))

# coalesce() only moves on to backup_amount when primary_clean is NA. 
# A recorded zero is a real, known value, so coalesce() keeps it instead of overwriting. 
# If this wasn't in place a legitimate value of "0" would be replaced.

reports_for_complete <- reports_clean %>%
  select(customer_id, round, amount) %>%
  mutate(recorded_row = TRUE)
 
n_original <- nrow(reports_for_complete)
n_missing_before <- sum(is.na(reports_for_complete$amount))

# One missing amount already exists before completion as C3, round 1. 
# An example of an absent customer-round combination that isn't in the table is C1, round 2.
 
reports_complete <- reports_for_complete %>%
  complete(customer_id, round = 1:3, fill = list(recorded_row = FALSE))
 
n_total_after <- nrow(reports_complete)
n_added <- n_total_after - n_original
n_missing_after <- sum(is.na(reports_complete$amount))
 
cat("Original rows:", n_original, "\n")
cat("Added rows:", n_added, "\n")
cat("Missing amounts before completion:", n_missing_before, "\n")
cat("Missing amounts after completion:", n_missing_after, "\n")
print(reports_complete)

```

# Part B

```{r}


cat("\nDuplicate customer IDs in customers:", anyDuplicated(customers$customer_id), "\n")
cat("Missing customer IDs in customers:", sum(is.na(customers$customer_id)), "\n")
 
dup_customer_rounds <- reports_clean %>% count(customer_id, round) %>% filter(n > 1)

print(dup_customer_rounds)
 
customers_marked <- customers %>% mutate(customer_found = TRUE)
 
reports_joined <- reports_clean %>%
  left_join(customers_marked, by = join_by(customer_id),
            relationship = "many-to-one", na_matches = "never") %>%
  mutate(customer_found = coalesce(customer_found, FALSE))
print(reports_joined %>% select(customer_id, round, amount, region, customer_found))
 
only_in_reports <- anti_join(reports_clean, customers, by = "customer_id", na_matches = "never") %>%
  distinct(customer_id)
only_in_customers <- anti_join(customers, reports_clean, by = "customer_id", na_matches = "never") %>%
  distinct(customer_id)
print(only_in_reports)
print(only_in_customers)

# C4 appears only in reports_clean, and 5 appears only in customers.
# The region for C3 is NA, but customer_found = TRUE tells us C3 is in the customer master file.
# C4 customer_found = FALSE tells us the NA region is not a blank field, but a complete absence of any master-file record at all.
 

```

# Part C

```{r}

# Because customers_bad has two rows for C1, each of C1's two reports matches both C1 rows and is duplicated, so row count rises from 6 to 8. 
# C1's original amounts get counted twice, which inflates the ignoring-NA total from 75 to 100 . 

 
# With relationship = "many-to-one", dplyr would raise an error. 
# This is because that setting asserts each report row matches at most one customer row, and C1 matches two. 
# Allowing "many-to-many" does not resolve the conflicting region values for C1 - it just silences the error and lets both conflicting rows pass through as duplicated output rows.
 
reports_wide <- reports_complete %>%
  select(customer_id, round, amount) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = round, values_from = amount, names_prefix = "round_")
print(reports_wide)
 
long_back <- reports_wide %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("round_"), names_to = "round",
               values_to = "amount", values_drop_na = TRUE)
cat("\nRows after pivot back with values_drop_na = TRUE:", nrow(long_back), "\n")

# Prediction: 5 rows. Of the 12 customer-round combinations in reports_complete, only 5 have a known amount. The other 7 are missing.

# values_drop_na = TRUE  removes rows with NA after reshaping it. It doesn't have any way to recover any known amounts, so those customer-rounds are just dropped from view.


```

# Problem 3 

# Part A

```{r}

two_sample_t <- function(x, y, equal_var = FALSE, alpha = 0.05) {
  nx <- length(x); ny <- length(y)
  mean_x <- mean(x); mean_y <- mean(y)
  var_x <- var(x); var_y <- var(y)
 
  if (equal_var) {
    sp2 <- ((nx - 1) * var_x + (ny - 1) * var_y) / (nx + ny - 2)
    se <- sqrt(sp2 * (1 / nx + 1 / ny))
    df <- nx + ny - 2
    method <- "Pooled"
  } else {
    se <- sqrt(var_x / nx + var_y / ny)
    df <- (var_x / nx + var_y / ny)^2 /
      ((var_x / nx)^2 / (nx - 1) + (var_y / ny)^2 / (ny - 1))
    method <- "Welch"
  }
 
  t_stat <- (mean_x - mean_y) / se
  p_value <- 2 * pt(abs(t_stat), df = df, lower.tail = FALSE)
  reject <- p_value < alpha
 
  list(method = method, t_stat = t_stat, df = df, p_value = p_value, reject = reject)
}
 
x_check <- c(12, 15, 14, 10, 13)
y_check <- c(9, 11, 8, 10, 7, 12, 9, 8)
 
ref_welch <- t.test(x_check, y_check, var.equal = FALSE)
ref_pooled <- t.test(x_check, y_check, var.equal = TRUE)
 
welch_result <- two_sample_t(x_check, y_check)
pooled_result <- two_sample_t(x_check, y_check, equal_var = TRUE)
print(welch_result)
print(pooled_result)
 
welch_diffs <- c(
  t_stat = abs(welch_result$t_stat - unname(ref_welch$statistic)),
  df     = abs(welch_result$df - unname(ref_welch$parameter)),
  p_value = abs(welch_result$p_value - ref_welch$p.value)
)
pooled_diffs <- c(
  t_stat = abs(pooled_result$t_stat - unname(ref_pooled$statistic)),
  df     = abs(pooled_result$df - unname(ref_pooled$parameter)),
  p_value = abs(pooled_result$p_value - ref_pooled$p.value)
)
print(welch_diffs)
print(pooled_diffs)
cat("All differences smaller than 1e-8:", all(c(welch_diffs, pooled_diffs) < 1e-8), "\n")


```

# Part B

```{r}

 
B <- 1000
n_x <- 20
n_y <- 40
alpha <- 0.05
 
scenarios <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("equal_null", "unequal_null",
               "equal_shift", "unequal_shift"),
  mean_x = c(0, 0, 0, 0),
  mean_y = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
  sd_x = c(1, 3, 1, 3),
  sd_y = c(1, 1, 1, 1)
)
 
# Run once immediately before the simulation, not inside a loop.
set.seed(2026)

```

```{r} 
n_scenarios <- nrow(scenarios)
total_rows <- n_scenarios * B * 2 
 
scenario_vec <- character(total_rows)
replicate_vec <- integer(total_rows)
method_vec <- character(total_rows)
t_stat_vec <- numeric(total_rows)
df_vec <- numeric(total_rows)
p_value_vec <- numeric(total_rows)
reject_vec <- logical(total_rows)
 
row_i <- 1
for (s in 1:n_scenarios) {
  for (b in 1:B) {
    x <- rnorm(n_x, mean = scenarios$mean_x[s], sd = scenarios$sd_x[s])
    y <- rnorm(n_y, mean = scenarios$mean_y[s], sd = scenarios$sd_y[s])
 
    res_welch <- two_sample_t(x, y, equal_var = FALSE, alpha = alpha)
    scenario_vec[row_i] <- scenarios$scenario[s]
    replicate_vec[row_i] <- b
    method_vec[row_i] <- res_welch$method
    t_stat_vec[row_i] <- res_welch$t_stat
    df_vec[row_i] <- res_welch$df
    p_value_vec[row_i] <- res_welch$p_value
    reject_vec[row_i] <- res_welch$reject
    row_i <- row_i + 1
 
    res_pooled <- two_sample_t(x, y, equal_var = TRUE, alpha = alpha)
    scenario_vec[row_i] <- scenarios$scenario[s]
    replicate_vec[row_i] <- b
    method_vec[row_i] <- res_pooled$method
    t_stat_vec[row_i] <- res_pooled$t_stat
    df_vec[row_i] <- res_pooled$df
    p_value_vec[row_i] <- res_pooled$p_value
    reject_vec[row_i] <- res_pooled$reject
    row_i <- row_i + 1
  }
}
 
simulation_results <- tibble(
  scenario = scenario_vec,
  replicate = replicate_vec,
  method = method_vec,
  t_stat = t_stat_vec,
  df = df_vec,
  p_value = p_value_vec,
  reject = reject_vec
)
 
print(head(simulation_results))
cat("Total rows in simulation_results:", nrow(simulation_results), "\n")
 
simulation_summary <- simulation_results %>%
  summarise(
    mean_t = round(mean(t_stat), 3),
    sd_t = round(sd(t_stat), 3),
    rejection_rate = round(mean(reject), 3),
    .by = c(scenario, method)
  )
print(simulation_summary)

plot_data <- simulation_summary %>%
  select(scenario, method, rejection_rate) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = rejection_rate)
plot_matrix <- t(as.matrix(plot_data[, c("Welch", "Pooled")]))
colnames(plot_matrix) <- plot_data$scenario
 
barplot(plot_matrix, beside = TRUE, ylim = c(0, 1),
        col = c("steelblue", "tomato"),
        main = "Rejection Rate by Scenario and Method",
        ylab = "Rejection rate", xlab = "Scenario")
abline(h = 0.05, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Welch", "Pooled"), fill = c("steelblue", "tomato"), bty = "n")


# Under both null scenarios Welch's rejection  rate stays close to 0.05 regardless of whether the population variances are equal.

# The Type I error is well controlled and the pooled test is also close to 0.05 when variances are equal. When unequal it goes above 0.05 once variances are meaning it rejects a true null. 

# When the  means differ by one unit, both tests' power rises far above 0.05. 

# The test rejects quite often and this only helps if its Type I error rate is also controlled. So results will vary slightly from run to run due to simulation randomness.

```
